title: 3-Read Friday #7: Time, the Planning Gap, and Mathematical Literacy
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Issue seven is united by the idea that investing time properly in a lesson's foundations pays that time back later. Barton opens with Paul Cline's "I haven't got time," which he calls a "powerful post" addressing teachers' most common complaint head-on, and summarizes Cline's argument that skipping prior-knowledge checks and worked examples to save time actually costs more time down the line. He then covers Pete Foster's "Filling the Planning Gap," highlighting Foster's use of Lemov's ratio concept and the idea of extending the "We Do" phase of a worked example before releasing students to independent practice. He closes with Amie Meek's piece on mathematical literacy, opening with the finding that weak readers struggle more in maths exams than in English Literature, and notes that choral response has become "a big change" in his own practice as a result. Barton explicitly draws the connecting thread himself: all three strategies "take more time in the moment, but should save lots of time in the long run."
points: Barton frames Cline's core argument as: spending more time on prior-knowledge checks and modelling now saves teachers more time later, reversing the usual time-pressure logic.
He credits Foster with extending the "We Do" phase of worked examples as a practical fix to ensure students are ready for independent practice.
He names choral response, drawn from Meek's post on mathematical literacy, as a technique that has become "a big change" in his own recent practice.
quotes: Wow, this is a powerful post that addresses head-on one of the most common complaints a teacher has: they don’t have enough time.
Paul makes a compelling argument that spending more time on things like these will save teachers more time in the long term.
The second is the idea of extending the We Do part of a worked example to ensure all students are at the point where they are ready to engage and thrive with independent practice.
This blog opens with a startling finding: weak readers struggle more in maths exams than in their English Literature exams.
There is a nice link with Paul’s blog above: these strategies take more time in the moment, but should save lots of time in the long run.
